title: Britain's aircraft carrier made of ice
caption:
In WW2 Britain seriously planned an aircraft carrier made of ice. 🧊🚢
Pykrete is ice frozen with about 14% wood pulp: the fibres stop cracks from spreading, so it is much tougher than plain ice and melts more slowly.
Would you have served on an ice ship? Yes or absolutely not?
first_comment: A warship you can fix with a freezer and a bag of sawdust. Genius or madness? 🧊🪵
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pykrete' and 'Project Habakkuk' (citing M. F. Perutz, 'Description of the Iceberg Aircraft Carrier', Journal of Glaciology, 1948): pykrete is about 14% wood pulp and 86% ice by weight, much stronger and slower-melting than ice; the planned ship was about 2,000 ft (610 m) long, kept frozen by refrigeration pipes; a small prototype was built at Patricia Lake, Alberta, in 1943; the project was abandoned as costs and steel requirements grew

The often-told demonstration in which a pistol shot shattered a block of ice but ricocheted off pykrete is reported in several accounts (Wikipedia 'Pykrete'), with differing details of who fired and where
